{{Short description|Iroquoian language spoken in eastern US}} {{Infobox language | name = Susquehannock | nativename = | states = [[United States]] | ethnicity = [[Susquehannock]] | familycolor = American | fam1 = [[Iroquoian languages|Iroquoian]] | fam2 = Northern | fam3 = Lake Iroquoian | fam4 = Five Nations | iso3 = sqn | glotto = susq1241 | glottorefname = Susquehannock | linglist = sqn | map = Susquehannock lang.png | mapcaption = Present Day Majority Distribution of the Conestoga Language (Susquehannock) | era = attested 1640s | altname = Conestoga | region = New York, Pennsylvania, Maryland, West Virginia ([[Northeastern United States]]) }} {{Portal|Language}} '''Susquehannock''', also known as '''Conestoga''', is an extinct [[Iroquoian languages|Iroquoian language]] spoken by the [[Indigenous peoples of the Americas|Native American]] people variously known as the [[Susquehannock]] or Conestoga. == Lexicon == Information about Susquehannock is scant. Almost all known words and phrases come from the ''Vocabula Mahakuassica'', a vocabulary written by the Swedish missionary [[John Campanius|Johannes Campanius]] in [[New Sweden]] during the 1640s and published by his grandson Thomas Campanius Holm in two separate works in 1696Johan Campanius. 1696. ''Catechismvs Lutheri Lingva Svecico-Americana: Lutheri Catechismus/ Öfwersatt på American-Virginiske Språket''. Stockholm: Burchardi Tryckeri af J. J. Genath. (Reprinted 1937 in Stockholm by Ivar Haeggström) and 1702.Thomas Campanius Holm. 1702. ''Kort beskrifning om provincien Nya Swerige uit America: Som nu förtjden af the Engelske kallas Pensylvania''. Stockholm: J.H. Werner for Sal. Wankijfs. [[Peter Stephen Du Ponceau]] translated the 1702 work from Swedish to English in 1834.Peter S. Du Ponceau. 1834. "A Short Description of the Province of New Sweden, Now Called, by the English, Pennsylvania, in America." Compiled From the Relations and Writings of Persons Worthy of Credit, and Adorned With Maps and Plates. By Thomas Campanius Holm. Translated from the Swedish, for the Historical Society of Pennsylvania. With Notes. By Peter S. Du Ponceau. ''Memoirs of the Historical Society of Pennsylvania'' 3:1-166. (Reprinted 1834 in Philadelphia by McCarty & Davis)
cited in Marianne Mithun. ''The Languages of Native America'' (1999, Cambridge University Press).{{Cite book |last=Holm |first=Thomas Campanius |title=A Vocabulary of Susquehannock |publisher=Evolution Publishing |year=2007 |isbn=9781889758855 |editor-last=Salvucci |editor-first=Claudio R. |edition=2nd |series=American Language Reprints |location=Merchantville, New Jersey, United States |pages=1–3 |language=en |translator-last=Duponceau |translator-first=Peter Stephen}} Campanius's vocabulary contains just over 100 words and phrases. Linguist [[Marianne Mithun]] believes this limited data is sufficient to classify Susquehannock as a Northern Iroquoian language, closely related to the languages of the [[Haudenosaunee Confederacy]].Marianne Mithun. 1981. "Stalking the Susquehannocks," ''International Journal of American Linguistics'' 47:1-26. Examples of Susquehannock-language place names include [[Conestoga River|Conestoga]], [[Juniata River|Juniata]], and [[Swatara Creek|Swatara]]. === Toponyms === Place names in the Conestoga homeland are documented as of Conestoga origin. After 1763, some Conestoga remnant peoples joined nations of the Haudenosaunee Confederacy, and the Conestoga language survived for a time. ''Indian Villages and Place Names in Pennsylvania with Numerous Historical Notes and References'' (1928), a book by Dr. George P.
